current_episode.title: Aerospace is Losing Key Electronics to Data Centers: How Executives Can Respond

guest.bio_context: Sebastian Shaw is an electrical engineer from the Technical University of Munich who studied as a Fulbright Scholar at Stanford for his second master's program. He co-founded Luminovo with Timon, also an electrical engineer from ETH Zurich, after both were exposed to the AI wave in 2015-2016 and built custom AI applications across automotive and semiconductor industries before focusing on electronics supply chain software.

pending_qa.q: How does electrification of traditional manufacturing sectors create demand for electronics supply chain solutions?
pending_qa.r: As mechanical companies transition to mechatronic companies by adding electronics to their product portfolios, their supply chain suddenly works differently. Electronics follow different laws of physics than plastics or mechanical components, with a tight connection between design and procurement that cannot simply transfer from mechanical blueprints. The aerospace and defense industry in particular is experiencing extreme booming with electrification, making companies desperate to gain control over their electronic supply chain.

pending_qa.q: What is driving the explosive growth in electronics component demand beyond historical trends?
pending_qa.r: Sebastian Shaw's analysis shows electronics spend has grown at roughly 7% compound annual growth rate over the last 20 years, projected to grow 10% year over year. The extra 3% growth comes exclusively from AI data centers. End of 2025 AI data center buildout is already the biggest infrastructure project inflation-adjusted ever undertaken, bigger than the U.S. railway system, motorway system, Apollo mission, and Manhattan Project combined, with $950 billion spent last year and another $700 billion this year.

pending_qa.q: Which electronic components face extreme supply constraints from AI data center competition?
pending_qa.r: Some components have 20x additional demand from pre-2022 levels due to AI data center buildout, and most supply chains cannot flex that fast. Publicly visible constraints affect DRAM and other smaller components like specific capacitors. If a product shares components with AI data centers, it faces real supply problems and companies need to re-architect their supply chain to avoid trouble in coming years.

pending_qa.q: Why is component obsolescence management particularly critical for aerospace and defense product lifespans?
pending_qa.r: Unlike consumer products with two-year lifespans, aerospace and defense product design lifespans are 10-20 years or longer. If a designer incorporates a component that a manufacturer like Texas Instruments will stop producing next year, the company faces deep trouble with recertification and other consequences. Active components with specific pin connections and internal logic cannot simply be substituted like mechanical parts, requiring either redesign or identifying alternative components from other vendors.

pending_qa.q: What is the scale of projected global AI data center spending through 2031?
pending_qa.r: Over the next years until 2030-2031, $7 trillion will be added to AI data center infrastructure spending according to Goldman Sachs, an 8x multiplier from current levels. This represents an unprecedented scale that will continue to pull components from other industries including aerospace and medical.

pending_qa.q: How does the current AI data center expansion differ fundamentally from previous supply chain disruptions like COVID-19?
pending_qa.r: Unlike COVID which was a shock with over-demand, recovery, and the typical bullwhip effect correction, the AI data center buildout is more like a black hole that was created that is not going to stop and will continue to suck up demand. It cannot be waited out because it represents sustained structural demand rather than a temporary surge.

pending_qa.q: What are the primary customer segments and value drivers for electronics supply chain software solutions?
pending_qa.r: Electronics OEM customers seek procurement and supply chain management for cost reduction and risk mitigation as a bottom-line project. EMS (contract manufacturing) companies generate both top-line impact by winning more business through higher-quality custom quotes and bottom-line impact through cost savings on components and internal process automation. Downstream suppliers and component distributors integrate as partners to gain exposure to the buying side.

pending_qa.q: What structural barriers exist to innovation adoption in electronics manufacturing?
pending_qa.r: Innovation diffuses at the rate of trust in the industry. While the industry operates at the forefront of innovation with their own products, they are often laggards when it comes to adopting innovation in their own internal processes. Gaining enough credibility and trust so that companies will actually listen to and implement transformative new products that improve their processes represents the primary bottleneck.

pending_qa.q: How can AI enable customization of enterprise software for diverse supply chain workflows?
pending_qa.r: By building on top of the domain model and software infrastructure, companies can now construct custom applications and workflows tailored to their specific needs. AI agents allow building custom views and functionality on top of the core platform, enabling companies to create their own specialized tools without waiting for the vendor to implement them, fundamentally changing how industry perceives what software can do.
